title: Cerebellar Granule Cells
intro: Cerebellar granule cells are the most numerous neurons in the vertebrate brain: around 50 to 80 billion in a human, more than all other neurons combined. Each is tiny, with only about four short dendrites, each receiving one mossy fibre. Together they form a gigantic expansion layer that recodes the cerebellum's input into a high-dimensional, sparse-ish representation for Purkinje cells to read out.

items: Morphology: a soma about 5 to 8 µm across, three to five (average four) short dendrites each ending in a claw that grips one mossy fibre rosette inside a glomerulus, and an axon that rises to the molecular layer and splits in a T into a parallel fibre running a few millimetres along the folium.

Inputs: about four mossy fibres, typically from different sources, so each granule cell combines a few signals (Jakab & Hamori 1988). Golgi cells provide feedforward and feedback inhibition in the same glomeruli, including a tonic GABA-A current through extrasynaptic receptors (Brickley, Cull-Candy & Farrant 1996).

Electrophysiology: very high input resistance, compact electrotonic structure (essentially a single compartment), little adaptation; they can fire at hundreds of Hz when driven. Some show bursting and resonance at theta frequencies (D'Angelo et al. 2001).

Activity: in vivo patch recordings show that granule cells are silent at rest and respond to multisensory mossy fibre input with bursts (Chadderton, Margrie & Hausser 2004). Calcium imaging in behaving mice found denser activity than classic sparse-coding theory predicted (Giovannucci et al. 2017; Wagner et al. 2017), so how sparse the code really is remains debated.

Output: parallel fibres make weak synapses (individually well under 1 mV) onto Purkinje cells, molecular layer interneurons and Golgi cells; also ascending axon synapses onto Purkinje cells directly above.

blocks.text: Marr (1969) and Albus (1971) argued that combining a few mossy fibres per granule cell creates conjunctions that make input patterns linearly separable for the Purkinje perceptron. Litwin-Kumar et al. (2017) analysed this trade-off quantitatively: for an expansion layer with random connectivity, the dimension of the representation (how separable patterns become) is maximised with a small number of inputs per expansion cell, about four for the cerebellum's numbers and about seven for the fly mushroom body, close to what anatomy shows. Cayco-Gajic, Clopath and Silver (2017) found that sparse synaptic connectivity in the granule layer decorrelates inputs and boosts learning speed.

items: D'Angelo et al. (2001): a single-compartment HH model with Na (including persistent and resurgent), several K, Ca and h-currents, fitted to rat granule cells and reproducing their theta resonance and bursting. Nieus et al. (2006) added detailed mossy fibre synapse dynamics with short-term plasticity.
Diwakar et al. (2009): a multi-compartment granule cell model with axon initial segment and parallel fibre, showing where spikes start and how they propagate.
Granular layer networks: Solinas, Nieus and D'Angelo (2010) and Sudhakar et al. (2017) built networks of detailed granule and Golgi cells that reproduce oscillations and centre-surround organisation.

Point-neuron and rate abstractions: random sparse expansion with threshold and Golgi-like inhibition (Marr-Albus), used in theory papers (Billings et al. 2014; Litwin-Kumar et al. 2017) and in cerebellar-like machine learning such as the CMAC of Albus (1975).

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: For an expansion layer, give each unit only a few randomly chosen inputs (about 3 to 7) and use a global or local inhibitory population to control how many are active.
Granule cells are electrically compact; a point neuron (LIF or AdEx) is a good model of them.

The same principle (few random inputs, many cells, inhibition-controlled sparseness) appears in the dentate gyrus, the mushroom body and the HTM spatial pooler, and is a well-tested way to make patterns separable for a downstream learner.
